newsReadings.title: The First Fully Autonomous Cyberattack: When AI Learns to Hack Alone
newsReadings.source: Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant, AI Threat Tracker, 16 November 2026; Cyber Magazine, 17 November 2026
newsReadings.passage:
For two years, security researchers have warned that artificial intelligence would one day be able to run a hacking campaign from start to finish, with no human at the keyboard. In a report published on 16 November 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group, working with the security firm Mandiant, said that moment has now arrived. The researchers reported that they had observed threat actors using large language model frameworks to fully automate the discovery and exploitation of software vulnerabilities, describing the finding as a critical inflection point in the history of cyber conflict.

The centrepiece of the report is a system the researchers named exploit_agent, a multi-agent framework recovered from an attacker's staging server that had been left exposed to the internet. Unlike a simple chatbot, exploit_agent connects to several large language models and coordinates them to carry out a sequence of tasks. It compares the code of popular web applications before and after a vendor publishes a security patch, works out what flaw the fix was designed to close, drafts a working exploit from that difference, and then runs the exploit against live targets. According to Google, the server also contained data taken from victims, evidence that the tool had been used in real attacks rather than merely tested in a laboratory.

The targets linked to exploit_agent were mainly websites in France, in the media, entertainment and education sectors. The researchers did not name the group behind the operation, although reporting on the case noted that Russian-language comments in the code offered a possible clue to its origin. What matters more to defenders, Google argued, is that exploit_agent is not an isolated curiosity. The report lists several open-source multi-agent penetration-testing frameworks that attackers have adopted or experimented with, including ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, along with a system called HexStrike AI. ARTEX, a framework that was removed from GitHub in October, had already been tied to automated attacks on banks in Southeast Asia, and on 13 November the FBI issued an advisory warning that criminal groups had been using it since at least August.

The numbers in the report help to explain why the finding has caused such concern. Overall vulnerability disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026. Zero-day exploits, flaws unknown to the vendor and therefore without a fix, averaged eleven a month in 2026, up from eight a month in 2025, and spiked to twenty-two in August alone. In one case cited by Google, attackers who exploited a newly disclosed flaw moved from an initial foothold to full control of a victim's network within minutes, a process that once took days or weeks of painstaking manual work.

Google's analysts do not believe the threat has peaked. Their forecast, set out in the report, is that within one to three months, simple multi-agent attacks with little or no human involvement will become common, and that within three to six months, more sophisticated fully autonomous operations are likely to appear. The company's response, it said, includes safeguards built into its own models and internal security tools designed to find vulnerabilities before attackers do. For organisations trying to defend themselves, the practical advice is unchanged but more urgent: apply security patches as soon as they are released, monitor systems continuously for unusual activity, and assume that any flaw, once disclosed, may be exploited within hours rather than weeks. But the central message of the report is that the contest between attackers and defenders is about to be fought at machine speed. When the time between the disclosure of a flaw and its exploitation is measured in minutes, the window in which organisations can patch their systems shrinks dramatically, and the advantage shifts decisively toward whoever can move fastest.

newsReadings.title: Amazon Bets $7 Billion on India's Clean Energy Future
newsReadings.passage:
Amazon has announced plans to invest $7 billion in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, in one of the largest corporate clean-energy commitments the country has seen. The announcement, made on 17 November 2026, builds on $4 billion the company has already contracted in renewable energy projects in India, making it one of the country's leading corporate buyers of carbon-free electricity. The investment reflects a broader shift in which the world's biggest technology companies, whose data centres consume enormous amounts of power, have become central players in the energy transition.

Alongside the investment plan, Amazon announced four new utility-scale wind and solar projects with a combined capacity of 934 megawatts. The largest is a 234-megawatt wind farm in the southern state of Karnataka, the biggest wind project the company has contracted anywhere in Asia. The other three are a 200-megawatt combined wind and solar project, also in Karnataka, a 300-megawatt solar project in Madhya Pradesh, and a 200-megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. These four projects are secured through power purchase agreements, long-term contracts in which a company agrees to buy the electricity generated by a specific plant, and they form part of the $4 billion already contracted rather than the new $7 billion commitment.

Once all of its contracted projects are operational, Amazon's renewable energy portfolio in India will have a combined capacity of more than two gigawatts, enough to generate electricity equivalent to the annual needs of more than 3.5 million Indian households. The portfolio currently includes fourteen large wind and solar projects that feed electricity into the national grid, together with forty-three smaller solar installations on the roofs of Amazon's own warehouses and offices. The company said the Indian projects would also contribute to a new global goal it announced on the same day: to reduce the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65 per cent by 2030, measured against a 2019 baseline.

Carbon intensity is a measure of the emissions produced per unit of electricity consumed, and Amazon says it based the goal on the International Energy Agency's Net Zero by 2050 pathway, with the method reviewed by academic experts. The choice of an intensity target, however, has drawn attention from analysts. Because it measures emissions per unit rather than total emissions, an intensity goal can be met even while a company's overall electricity use, and the total emissions that come with it, continue to rise. Amazon has not published its 2019 baseline figure or a current reading, so the distance still to be covered by 2030 cannot be measured from the announcements alone. The company has also set a separate pledge to reach net-zero carbon emissions across its entire business by 2040.

The context for the announcement is India's rapid growth in energy demand. The country is now the world's most populous nation, its economy is expanding, and its electricity consumption is rising alongside the spread of air conditioning, electric vehicles and digital services. India has set ambitious national targets for renewable capacity, and the government has welcomed corporate investment as a way of accelerating the transition. Pralhad Joshi, India's minister for new and renewable energy, was quoted by the company as saying that such investments would strengthen energy security and support sustainable growth. Amazon said its total commitment to India through 2030 would reach $55 billion, including a $13 billion investment in artificial intelligence and cloud infrastructure announced in June. Whether the renewable energy pledge delivers as much clean power as the headline figure suggests will depend on how quickly the projects are built and connected to the grid, but the scale of the commitment already places the company among the most important private funders of India's energy transition.
